query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Using a liquid‐phase precursor method to synthesize nanoscale ZrB2 powders followed by rapid densification (e.g., spark plasma sintering at ~1800°C) will produce a denser, less porous single‐phase ZrB2 ceramic that is more resistant to degradation during prolonged liquid plating exposure compared to conventionally sintered samples at >2300°C.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional single‐phase ZrB2 produced at >2300°C, which exhibits relatively high porosity and residual defects that contribute to liquid plating bath induced damage.
generation.intervention: Switch the processing route to a liquid-phase precursor method to achieve molecular-level mixing and nanoscale powder synthesis, then densify the powders via spark plasma sintering at a reduced temperature (~1800°C).
generation.conditions: Powders prepared via a controlled liquid precursor (impregnation pyrolysis) method under an inert or reducing atmosphere; sintering performed under SPS conditions at approximately 1800°C with short dwell times; subsequent exposure tests conducted under typical liquid plating bath conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a refined microstructure due to nanoscale particle size and homogeneous distribution achieved via the liquid precursor route, which minimizes pore formation and enhances grain boundary bonding during densification.
generation.mechanism: The liquid precursor method ensures intimate mixing of reactants at a molecular scale, thus lowering the activation energy for densification. When combined with the rapid heating and short dwell time inherent in SPS, a fully sintered, dense ceramic forms at a lower temperature, reducing the formation of defects (holes) that facilitate liquid ingress in plating baths.
generation.predicted_outcome: The proposed method will yield ZrB2 ceramics with mechanical strength comparable to or exceeding that of conventionally sintered materials, while showing a noticeably reduced porosity and fewer microstructural weaknesses. Consequently, the ceramics will exhibit higher resistance to the mechanisms of degradation (hole formation) during prolonged liquid plating bath exposure.
generation.baseline: Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 processed at temperatures above 2300°C, which typically shows higher porosity and microstructural flaws that lead to premature component failure under prolonged plating treatment.
generation.boundary: Preparation: Sintering temperature lowered from >2300°C to around 1800°C using the liquid-phase precursor/SPS approach. Service: Long-duration exposure to liquid plating baths under conditions relevant to operational environments.
generation.uncertainty: While initial evidence from analogous systems supports that liquid precursor methods can reduce processing temperatures and improve densification, the exact improvement in long-term structural integrity against plating bath-induced degradation in ZrB2 ceramics remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of ZrB2 ceramic samples: one using the conventional sintering process at >2300°C and the other using the liquid precursor method followed by SPS at ~1800°C. Characterize both sets for density, porosity, and mechanical strength. Then subject the samples to a controlled long-duration liquid plating bath exposure. Compare pre- and post-exposure microstructural integrity and extent of damage (e.g., hole formation).
measurements: Density and porosity measurements (using the Archimedes method or mercury intrusion porosimetry)
Mechanical strength testing (e.g., flexural or compressive strength tests)
Microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM to assess grain boundaries and pore distribution) before and after plating bath exposure
Quantitative assessment of surface degradation and hole formation (e.g., image analysis or weight loss measurements) after long-duration exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ZrB2 samples produced by the liquid precursor/SPS method do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in porosity, improved mechanical strength, and lower degradation (hole formation) following plating bath exposure compared to the conventional samples, then the hypothesis must be rejected.

Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni Oxide as a Highly Efficient Thermoelectric High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: Among the existing materials for heat conversion, high-entropy alloys are of great interest due to the tunability of their functional properties. Here, we aim to produce single-phase high-entropy oxides composed of Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni-O through spark plasma sintering (SPS), testing their thermoelectric (TE) properties. This material was successfully obtained before via a different technique, which requires a very long processing time. Hence, the main target of this work is to apply spark plasma sintering, a much faster and scalable process. The samples were sintered in the temperature range of 1200–1300 °C. Two main phases were formed: rock salt-structured Fm3̅m and spinel-structured Fd3̅m. Synthesis and Characterization of High-Purity, High-Entropy Diboride Ceramic Powders by a Liquid Phase Method

Abstract: AbstractA nano-dual-phase powder with ultra-fine grain size was synthesized by the liquid precursor method at 1200 °C. A series of single-phase high-entropy ceramic powders ((Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Mo)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta, Mo)B2) with high purity (C content less than 0.9 wt% and O content less than 0.7 wt%) and ultrafine (average grain sizes of 340–570 nm) were successfully synthesized at 1800 °C. The sample of (TiZrHfNbTa)B2 exhibited a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure, and the metal elements were uniformly distributed at the nanoscale, microscale, and macroscale. This method did not apply to the preparation of all high-entropy ceramic powders and was unfavorable for the formation of single-phase high-entropy borides when the size difference factor exceeded 3.9%. The present work provides a guide for the development of ceramic-based composites through precursor impregnation pyrolysis.Keywords: liquid-phase precursor method, high-entropy diboride powders, solid solutions, microstructure, pyrolysis mechanism
